newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia farmers may sue government in land row.
newsitem.headline: Australia farmers may sue government in land row.

text.p: Australian farmers on Wednesday threatened to sue Australia's federal and state governments for compensation for lost earnings and lower land values because of native title claims on pastoral properties.

They also raised the spectre of escalating competing lawsuits against governments by native title claimants and farmers, with compensation claims by farmers through the courts making aboriginal claims look "miniscule".

The New South Wales Farmers Association fired the latest shot in the saga over native title claims on Australian pastoral lease land by issuing a statement threatening massive compensation claims against government over the Wik decision.

In this, Australia's High Court last December ruled that native title and pastoral leases could co-exist, leaving 78 percent of Australia's 7.68 million square kilometres (2.96 million square miles) potentially claimable by aborigines under native title laws.
"Basically yes, that's the bottom line," NSW Farmers Association spokesman Chris Brown said when asked if the farmers were threatening to sue the government.
Threatened legal suits against government for compensation had been raised in a letter to Prime Minister John Howard in recent days, he said.
A spokesman for Howard told Reuters the Prime Minister would meet with Queensland Premier Rob Borbidge and aboriginal delegates on Thursday and would meet with state premiers next week.
"Negotiations with stakeholders are continuing," he said.

Australian farmers see financial losses resulting from being prevented from changing land use by native title holders and want the federal government to extinguish native title on pastoral leases, senior vice president of the NSW Farmers Association, John Cobb, said in a statement issued on Wednesday.

Statements by Brown to Reuters showed that the farmers saw possible legal action through precedents under which governments encouraged diversification of rural activities on pastoral leasehold land and which effectively valued pastoral leasehold land on freehold terms.
Native title claims would affect leasehold values, he said.

They would require negotiation by farmers with native title claimants if wheat were to be planted on grazing land, he said. The power of native title claimants to refuse agreement could affect the value of pastoral leases.
"If that happens we will seek compensation from the government for losses caused by that," he said.
Established law was that pastoral leasehold land was traded at freehold values, "it is in effect freehold," Brown said.
Cobb said in the statement that leasehold farmers in NSW under state law had paid freehold equivalent value for their properties, in many cases many hundreds of thousands of dollars.
"Any action by the parliament that prevents farmers from diversifying their activities in the future, resulting in a fall in land values, will leave governments open to compensation claims," he said.
"A government worried about compensation claims from aborigines (which) holds back farming development as a result will be the subject of farmers compensation claims," he said.

For decades governments had allowed farmers to diversify their farming operations away from grazing to incorporate such activities as cotton, rice, cereal, grape, dairy, citrus and vegetable production for sustainable development, he said.
Cobb also said restricting what farmers could do on their land by codifying activities in legislation would leave governments opern to future compensation claims.
Last Friday, aboriginal groups threatened to seek international trade sanctions against Australia over its treatment of native land rights.
